TITLE: Investigating the effectiveness of intermediate activation as a communication medium
PROPOSAL: We will modify the AC protocol to transmit multiple intermediate activations at different layers, instead of just the last token's hidden state. We will compare the performance of this modified AC protocol to the original AC protocol on various real-world tasks.
CONTROLS: We will use CIPHER and explicit natural language communication as baselines for comparison. We will also ablate the protocol by comparing the performance of the receiver with and without the additional activations.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified AC protocol should show better performance than the original AC protocol, especially on tasks that require more complex reasoning, such as multi-hop question answering and mathematical problem solving. However, it may be more computationally expensive and require more fine-tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the representation quality of different internal information for communication
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the representation quality of different internal information used for communication, such as token embeddings, attention weights, and intermediate activations, using techniques like dimensionality reduction and feature importance analysis. We will analyze the correlation between the representation quality and the performance of various communication protocols.
CONTROLS: We will compare the representation quality of the different internal information used by CIPHER, AC, and explicit natural language communication. We will also ablate the communication protocol by using a random subset of the internal information as the communication medium.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that certain internal information, such as attention weights or intermediate activations, are more effective for communication than others, such as token embeddings. This will provide insights for designing more effective communication protocols.

PREDICTION: We expect to find that the choice of weights in CIPHER has a significant impact on the representation quality and communication performance, and that careful selection of weights can lead to significant improvements.

TITLE: Exploring the effect of task complexity on communication protocol performance
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of various communication protocols, including CIPHER, AC, and explicit natural language communication, on a range of tasks with varying complexity, such as multi-hop question answering and mathematical problem solving. We will analyze how the protocols perform under different levels of task complexity and identify any patterns or trends.

PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of the various communication protocols (CIPHER, AC, and the proposed end-to-end trainable protocol) on multi-agent tasks such as scientific paper question answering, mathematical problem solving, and dialogue summarization, using real-world datasets and benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the different protocols on each task, using metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and ROUGE score. We will also analyze the relevance of the communication protocols to each task.
COST: 300 GPU-hours

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Canonical Communication Protocols: CIPHER and AC
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of CIPHER and AC on three real-world datasets: SQuAD (single-hop QA), HotpotQA (multi-hop QA), and TrivialQA (dialogue summarization). For each dataset, we will compare these two protocols against a baseline that uses explicit language communication. We will measure the performance using the F1-score, Exact Match, and ROUGE-L metrics.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: explicit language communication
2. Baseline - Ablation: sender LLM and receiver LLM with no intervention (i.e., no communication)
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CIPHER and AC may perform better than the baseline on tasks that require rich contextual understanding, but may struggle with tasks that require fine-grained detailed information. They may also require more training data and capacity than the baseline. The implicit communication protocols may fail in tasks with crucial context clues that are only present in the explicit communication process.

PROPOSAL: We will revamp this experiment to compare the performance of CIPHER and AC on the same three datasets (SQuAD, HotpotQA, and TrivialQA), in addition to evaluating their ability to handle long context passages (up to 10,000 tokens) using the long-document QA datasets PubMedQA and BioASQ.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: explicit language communication
2. Baseline - Ablation: sender LLM and receiver LLM with no intervention (i.e., no communication)
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CIPHER and AC may demonstrate better performance with increased context passage length, but may require further fine-tuning to adapt to specific domains (e.g., scientific text). This evaluation will also help identify limitations in their current design, which might lead to the development of more robust communication protocols.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Transformers for Intermediate Representation Communication
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of different transformer architectures (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa, Longformer) as intermediate representation communicators. Specifically, we will experiment with using the last token's hidden state (as in AC) and different pooling mechanisms (e.g., mean, max, attention-weighted) to transmit information between models.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: using a fixed transformer architecture (e.g., BERT) as in AC
2. Baseline - Ablation: varying the size of the input context
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Different transformer architectures and pooling mechanisms may exhibit varying degrees of communication efficiency and effectiveness, with some potentially outperforming AC in specific tasks and others failing to improve upon it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Token Embedding Communication
PROPOSAL: We will develop and evaluate an adaptive token embedding communication protocol, where the sender model identifies and communicates the most relevant tokens to the receiver model. For this purpose, we will use a mask vector and learn a reconstruction loss between the original and communicated tokens to measure the faithfulness of the information transmitted.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: using a fixed set of token embeddings (e.g., CIPHER)
2. Baseline - Ablation: varying the number of tokens transmitted
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive token embedding communication protocol may offer improved effectiveness in transmitting relevant information, but may require significant increases in model capacity and training time. It may also struggle with tasks that require fine-grained understanding of the input tokens.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Low-Rank Communication
PROPOSAL: We will investigate efficient low-rank communication methods, where the sender and receiver models factorize the communication matrix into lower-dimensional sparse components. We will explore various factorization methods (e.g., singular value decomposition (SVD), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF)) to identify the most efficient and effective approach.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: using a full-rank communication matrix (e.g., CIPHER)
2. Baseline - Ablation: varying the rank of the factorized matrix
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Efficient low-rank communication methods may significantly reduce the communication overhead while maintaining or even improving the effectiveness of the communication protocol, but may require careful tuning of the factorization method and rank parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Communication Protocol for Multi-Agent Systems
PROPOSAL: We will develop and evaluate a regularized communication protocol that incorporates a regularizer term to the cross-entropy loss to encourage the sender model to communicate a subset of relevant information to the receiver model. Specifically, we will use a statistical entropy loss as the regularizer to measure the information content of the transmitted tokens.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: using a standard cross-entropy loss for communication (e.g., CIPHER)
2. Baseline - Ablation: varying the strength of the entropy regularizer
COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The regularized communication protocol may help the sender model strategically select the most relevant information for transmission, resulting in improved communication efficiency and effectiveness, but may require careful tuning of the regularization strength.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Grounded Communication: Leveraging Task-Specific Knowledge
PROPOSAL: We will investigate a grounded communication approach that leverages task-specific knowledge to inform the communication process between the sender and receiver models. Specifically, we will use a graph neural network-based method to identify key knowledge entities and relationships relevant to the task, and then use this information to select the most relevant information for communication.
CONTROLS: 
1. Baseline: using a standard communication protocol (e.g., CIPHER)
2. Baseline - Ablation: varying the coverage of the graph neural network
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The grounded communication approach may significantly improve the effectiveness of communication by providing task-specific context to the sender and receiver models, but may require careful development of the graph neural network architecture and training procedures.

ACTION: ADD
title: exploring communication protocols for efficient multi-agent learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to experiment with a range of communication protocols that leverage internal representations of language models, including weighted averages of token embeddings (CIPHER), transmission of intermediate activations (AC), and transmitting the output of a intermediate layer in the sender model. We will explore these methods on a range of tasks from multi-hop question answering to scientific paper question answering.
CONTROLS: Baseline - no communication between models; Baseline + natural language communication between models; CIPHER and AC as implemented in existing literature.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours ( approx 40 experiments with 25 training iterations each)
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in performance compared to no communication, and compared to natural language communication, particularly for complex tasks. CIPHER may be most effective for multi-agent learning, while AC and intermediate layer transmission may be more effective for tasks requiring fine-grained control. However, CIPHER may face challenges in terms of the loss of information during transmission.
